Jurassic English · Level 5 Teacher Pack


Level 5 Curriculum Overview
Ages 15+ · CEFR B2+–C1 · 40 lessons. Nine four-lesson story cycles lead to a four-lesson intertextual capstone
anchored in the tenth JE story. All ten original six-chapter storybooks are required; no third-party novel is
required. Introduce and read the tenth anchor before Lesson 37. The Lesson 4 pairing is an optional extension
only when that text has already been introduced and read.


Sequence
    Lessons   JE core text                        Focus

    1–4       A Box Called Other                  Categories, agency and the limits of a tidy record

    5–8       The Heron Stamp                     Internal exclusion, external pressure and cultural continuity

    9–12      The Names on the Tarpaulin          Witness, displaced lives and the misuse of evidence

    13–16     A Proof of Her Own                  Education, belonging and earned uncertainty

    17–20     The Workshop Without                Gendered access, safety and who can close an opening
              Windows

    21–24     The Map Beneath the Map             Living bodies, administrative space and plural memory

    25–28     Two Accounts of the Crossing        Imagination, uncertainty and evidence under disruption

    29–32     Permission to Repair                Satire, circular approval and useful rules

    33–36     The Jacket with Two Linings         Public identity, repair and the grammar of a finished past

    37–40     The Credit We Owed                  Accountability, unequal credit and repair without guaranteed
                                                  reconciliation


Progression and evidence
Term 1, Lessons 1–13: sentence-level language analysis, claims and source limits; retain the Lesson 12 closing
artifact. Term 2, Lessons 14–27: counter-argument and distinct dual warrants; Lesson 27 is the independent
milestone. Term 3, Lessons 28–40: two contributing JE evidence streams in synthesis, then a 400–600 word
capstone. Lessons 37–40 are pairing/outline, draft, reverse-engineering/peer review and defence/final revision.
Most lessons run 45 minutes. Lessons 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8 and 9 use a full 60-minute plan; Lessons 2, 6 and 10 have a
45-minute core plus optional 15-minute feedback. Do not silently squeeze a 60-minute plan into 45 minutes; split
it over two meetings and record the split.

Jurassic English · Level 5 Teacher Pack

Support: pre-highlight anchors and supply part of the cultural chain, recording help used. Core: independent
paragraph or full essay with exact evidence. Extension: add a third text or test a counter-case, keeping every
source necessary. Provide enlarged text, pre-cut or numbered move cards, dictation, movement choices and
private/written participation. Host roles are voluntary and rotated. Cutting and auditory proofreading both have
quiet visual alternatives.


7. Assessment and reporting
Share the four-level rubric before writing. Assess evidence accuracy, language mechanism, distinct warrants,
counter-reasoning, cohesion and scope. Keep access notes separate. One missing move becomes the next
feedback target. Retain a Term 1 syntactic artifact, the Lesson 27 independent dual-warrant artifact, a Term 3
synthesis and the capstone with drafts. Moderate a sample across teachers using the actual work and support
record. A completion certificate is not language certification.
The core capstone target is 400–600 words. Support may use a 350–450 word practice draft and extra time;
label it as supported practice and provide a route to the full core submission. Do not fill in a successful word
count on behalf of a learner.


8. Implementation and troubleshooting
Fast checks: do learners have both named stories, the right chapter and the correct lesson page? If a quotation
differs, return to the printed chapter before discussing its meaning. If warrants merge, draw two chains: evidence
→ voice/access rule; evidence → named material process. If ecological language is generic, ask which physical
system and what assessment is missing. If debate stalls, read the strongest rival anchor and ask what it can
establish. If cognitive load is high, reduce the number of simultaneous moves and restore them one at a time.
Treatment means a feasible response to test, not compulsory optimism or a cure. Give the action an owner, a
check and a trade-off. Respect unresolved disagreement. Never require handling chemicals, batteries, damaged
structures or hazardous sites as part of a language exercise. Use printed descriptions or safe classroom models
only.


9. Sources and contemporary transfer
All practice case cards here are expressly fictional. For factual transfer, a teacher must supply an already verified
offline source with organisation/author, date, title, locator, method and limitation. Check what it actually
establishes; separate association from causation and projections from observations. If no factual source is
supplied, use the fictional practice card and mark factual comparison not completed. Do not invent a statistic,
scientific result, quotation, historical reception or current case. Never present literary fiction as measurement.


10. Timing and capstone logistics
The three 12-minute drafting blocks fit inside the 45-minute Lesson 38 plan. Each of the first two includes a final
30-second reset. The workbook records progress; the full draft uses additional paper. Lesson 39 peer feedback is
six minutes per partner plus a recording minute, not two eight-minute turns in a thirteen-minute slot. Lesson 40
uses circles of 4–5 within the seminar block so every learner can respond. Indoor observation is equivalent to an
outdoor reset. Record extensions honestly rather than claim an overfilled lesson was completed.

Jurassic English · Teacher Book · Level 5                                                                                               A Box Called Other


How to teach this book
Thinking Cycle, quick path, two-week unit plan, chant and phonics

The Jurassic Thinking Cycle has four steps. In this book each step is tied to one chapter. Learners meet it on
student page 18.

 Step                Chapter        What learners do

   Analyze           3              Excavation · Noor writes two drafts of one sentence. What the author does here is set a
                                    passive version beside an active one. What does the passive draft, ‘Waiting responses were
                                    not represented’, do?
                                    Answer: A. It hides who made the omission, so the gap looks natural
                                    Clue: It also made the omission harder to mistake for a natural feature of the data.

   Evaluate          3              Strata · What produced the absence in the first chart? Gather evidence for each reading,
                                    including at least one quotation from an opposing voice such as Harun, give each reading a
                                    weight from 0 to 10, then choose one to defend while acknowledging the alternative.
                                    Choices: The form’s three categories made the absence almost inevitable / The people
                                    summarising chose what to display, so the choice made the gap / Ordinary constraints
                                    combined to create an effect nobody intended. Any view supported by a story clue.

   Justify           4              CEIW+Impact with a Dual Warrant · Defend your reading: a contested Claim, cited Evidence
                                    (one quotation from an opposing voice), an Interpretation of technique, a Cultural and an
                                    Ecological Warrant, a counterargument you refute, and a specific real-world Impact.
                                    Word bank: on page, What the author does here is, This suggests that, because, Someone might
                                    argue, passive voice, agency, category, omission, shaded place, systemic

   Reflect           4              Impact · Noor argued that the omission removed evidence of everyday use of a shaded
                                    place. Choose one real kind of public decision, such as redesigning a square or removing a
                                    tree, and trace what could happen to people and to the non-human world (trees, soil, heat,
                                    birds) when a record leaves out how a place is used. Propose one intervention and one
                                    measurable check that would show whether the record improved.
                                    Answers vary: open to the learner’s own experience.


Quick path: three sessions

  Session 1 · Excavation: syntax, rhetoric, irony and point of view · 35 min
   1. Read chapters 1–3 of A Box Called Other aloud; learners answer each chapter question and point to the
      exact clue.
   2. Excavate syntax: compare the passive caption ‘miscellaneous responses had been excluded for clarity’ with
      Noor’s active rewrite in chapter 3. Who acts in each sentence, and who disappears?
   3. Excavate irony and point of view: a chart excluded answers ‘for clarity’; a spreadsheet ‘seemed to promise
      that every answer could find a place’. Learners explain each technique with “What the author does here
      is…”.
   4. Pairs complete the Analyze step, then separate two claims as the story does: the form shaped the record,
      which is not the same as controlling what Eda thinks.
